question: What is dependency injection and why use it on Android?
answer:
Dependency injection (DI) means giving an object its collaborators from outside, rather than letting it construct or look them up itself.

Why it matters on Android:
• Testability — swap a real service for a fake in a unit test without touching the class under test.
• Explicit dependencies — the constructor signature is the complete list of what a class needs.
• Lifetime control — singleton vs per-screen vs per-feature is decided in one place instead of in scattered `getInstance()` calls.
• It removes the service-locator anti-pattern, where a class reaches into a global to find what it needs and nothing in its signature says so.

Approaches:
• Manual DI — plain constructor injection with a container built in `Application.onCreate`. Perfectly fine for a small app and worth knowing, because every framework is doing this for you.
• Hilt — Google's recommended framework, built on Dagger 2. Annotation-driven, generated at compile time, and it knows about Android lifecycles (`@HiltViewModel`, `@AndroidEntryPoint`).
• Dagger 2 — the full toolkit with manual components and subcomponents. More boilerplate; used where Hilt's fixed component tree is not enough.
• Koin — a runtime DSL with no code generation. Easy to start with, but a missing binding fails when the screen opens rather than when you build. `koin-annotations` adds KSP-generated modules and compile-time checks.
• kotlin-inject and Kodein — niche; kotlin-inject is the usual pick when the object graph has to be Kotlin Multiplatform.

question: What is Hilt? How does it differ from Dagger 2?
answer:
Hilt is Google's official DI library for Android, and it is Dagger 2 with the component tree already written for you.

• Entry points are annotations: `@HiltAndroidApp` on the Application, `@AndroidEntryPoint` on Activity/Fragment/Service, `@HiltViewModel` on ViewModels, `hiltViewModel()` in Compose.
• The component hierarchy is predefined and mapped to Android lifecycles — SingletonComponent, ActivityRetainedComponent, ActivityComponent, ViewModelComponent, FragmentComponent, ServiceComponent.
• `@InstallIn(...)` says which component a module belongs to, so a module is added by declaring it rather than by being listed in a component interface.
• You never write `Component` or `Subcomponent` interfaces, and you never hand-wire an Activity to its component.

Dagger 2 is still doing the work underneath, and Hilt does not hide it: `@Module`, `@Provides`, `@Binds`, `@Qualifier` and multibindings are all Dagger. If you need a custom component with a lifetime Android does not have, you drop to `@DefineComponent` or plain Dagger; most apps never do.

Setup is the `com.google.dagger.hilt.android` Gradle plugin plus `ksp("com.google.dagger:hilt-compiler")`. Hilt's processor runs under KSP now; kapt still works but is legacy, roughly doubles annotation-processing time and drags in the old compiler frontend.

Choosing: greenfield goes to Hilt. A large existing Dagger codebase can migrate gradually, since the two coexist in one build.

question: What are scopes in Hilt and how do they map to component lifecycles?
answer:
A Hilt scope pins a binding to the lifetime of one Android component, from the whole application down to a single ViewModel.

• `@Singleton` → SingletonComponent — one instance for the process.
• `@ActivityRetainedScoped` → ActivityRetainedComponent — survives configuration changes; the same lifetime as the ViewModelStore, so it lives from the first `onCreate` until the Activity really finishes.
• `@ActivityScoped` → ActivityComponent — one per Activity instance, so a rotation gives you a new one.
• `@FragmentScoped` → FragmentComponent.
• `@ViewModelScoped` → ViewModelComponent — one instance shared by the collaborators of a single `@HiltViewModel`, released when that ViewModel is cleared.
• `@ServiceScoped` → ServiceComponent.

An unscoped binding is created fresh at every injection point, and that is the correct default. Scope only what holds state that must be shared, or what is genuinely expensive to build.

Two things that bite in interviews. A scoped binding that holds an Activity `Context` outlives the Activity and leaks it — inject `@ApplicationContext` unless you truly need the Activity one. And a binding in a wider component cannot depend on one in a narrower component: a `@Singleton` cannot take an `@ActivityScoped` type, which is the usual cause of a "cannot be provided" build error.

question: What are @Qualifier and multibinding in Dagger/Hilt?
answer:
A `@Qualifier` tells Dagger which of several bindings of the same type you mean, and multibinding collects many bindings into one `Set` or `Map`.

Qualifiers — annotate both the binding and the injection point with the same annotation:
• Several `OkHttpClient` instances (authenticated vs plain).
• Dispatchers: `@IoDispatcher`, `@MainDispatcher`, `@DefaultDispatcher`. Injecting the dispatcher is what makes a class testable with a test dispatcher.
• Several Retrofit instances against different base URLs.
Prefer a real qualifier annotation over `@Named("io")` — a typo in a string is a runtime surprise, a typo in an annotation is a compile error.

Multibinding — contribute into a collection that Dagger assembles:
• `@IntoSet` adds the binding to `Set<T>`.
• `@IntoMap` with `@StringKey("...")` or `@ClassKey(...)` adds it to a `Map<K, V>`.
• Inject the collection as `Set<@JvmSuppressWildcards T>`, or Kotlin's variance turns it into `Set<? extends T>` and Dagger cannot match it.

Multibinding is what makes feature modules composable: each feature contributes its navigation routes, its settings entries or its initializers, and the app module gets the union without ever importing the features. `Map<Class<*>, Provider<ViewModel>>` is the same mechanism that Dagger-based ViewModel factories were built on before Hilt.

question: How do you replace dependencies in tests with Hilt?
answer:
Hilt provides the `@HiltAndroidTest` rule and `@TestInstallIn` / `@UninstallModules` to swap real bindings for fakes in instrumented tests.

For plain unit tests, do not involve Hilt at all — construct the ViewModel or Repository with fakes directly. That is faster, simpler, and it keeps the test independent of the DI graph.

For instrumented and Compose UI tests:
• Annotate the test class `@HiltAndroidTest` and add `HiltAndroidRule` as rule order 0, before the Compose rule, then call `hiltRule.inject()` in `@Before`.
• Replace a whole module with `@TestInstallIn(components = [...], replaces = [...])` in the test source set — the modern way; the replacement applies to every test that sees it.
• `@UninstallModules(NetworkModule::class)` on one test class removes a module for that class only, when you need a one-off.
• `@BindValue` on a test field binds that exact instance into the graph, which is the quickest way to hand a test its own fake and then assert on it afterwards.
• The whole app needs a test runner that creates `HiltTestApplication` (a custom `AndroidJUnitRunner`), or nothing is injected.

For Compose, host the screen in a `ComponentActivity` annotated `@AndroidEntryPoint` declared in the debug manifest, and drive it with `createAndroidComposeRule`.

question: Hilt vs Koin — when to choose which?
answer:
Hilt buys compile-time verification of the whole object graph; Koin buys a plain Kotlin DSL and no code generation.

Hilt:
• KSP code generation — a missing, duplicated or miscoped binding fails the build, never a user's phone.
• No reflection and no runtime lookup, so resolution costs nothing at startup.
• First-party integration with Jetpack: ViewModel, Navigation, Compose, WorkManager.
• More annotations to learn, and build time grows with the graph.

Koin:
• A module is just a Kotlin function; nothing to generate, nothing to wait for.
• Runtime resolution — a missing binding throws when the screen opens, not when you build. `verify()` and `koin-annotations` (KSP) recover some of that safety.
• Multiplatform: the same modules work in a shared KMP module, where Hilt cannot go at all.
• Lower barrier to entry, less ergonomic once you need real scoping across many modules.

Choosing:
• Android-only app, one team, greenfield → Hilt, the official path.
• Shared KMP module → Koin (or kotlin-inject); Hilt is Android-only.
• Large codebase with many feature modules → Hilt, for the build-time guarantees and multibinding.
• Prototype or learning project → Koin, for the lower ceremony.

Either way the classes themselves should take their dependencies through the constructor, which keeps the choice reversible.
